en: All the watching Muslims
Started and grew afraid.
Algara beneath him,
When it chased a three-year-old, never let it escape;
Its tail was sparse and its mane was scant,
And it was practiced against a fighting foe.
The foot of its tether stood on blue stone.
The people marveled and roared;
The Black Chinese and many Manchus
Raised a clamorous shout.
The Muslim people lamented;
The Black Chinese and many Manchus
Raised a crying shout.
When they saw Kongurbay's form,
Khan Koshoy of Katagan
And saintly hero Bakay
Saw the monstrous size
Of hero Kongurbay the infidel.
"Kongurbay of the Chinese
Has perfect fortune;
He is a hero who knows
The enemy's devices perfectly.
Kongurbay, son of Alooke,
Has all twelve limbs in proportion.
He is a hero of towering stature.
Whoever grapples with him cannot survive;
He is at the height of his power.
The renowned hero Kalcha—
If a hero comes out to fight him,
Will he arrive before an arrow?
Will he reach and crush him?
Will he offer him as a sacrifice?
Will he take his ancient revenge?"
Lord Koshoy and Khan Bakay
Saw him and despaired of life.
When they saw Kongurbay's form,
Golden-crested, with tasseled belt,
Only son of Khan Azoozil,
Wearing a coat of yellow gold
And mounted on a piebald horse,
With a decorated belt around his neck,
Pleaded with the Muslims,
Saying, "Let me enter the joust.
My uncle, old Koshoy,
You elders stand here;
You palmful of Muslims,
All of you stand here.
What I amassed remains in Kakanchyn;
What I have chosen is my faith.
What I amassed remains in Beijing;
What I pledged is my faith.
My Prophet is true, my religion is true;
The golden throne was left in Beijing.
When I renounced it and scattered it,
Turned from the black faith to the true one,
And fled as a Muslim,
The Chinese were a multitude and I was alone.
What deed have I done before God?
Barely escaping death,
Leaving my martyred mother behind,
All the Chinese and many Manchus
Came out to block me and fought.
From the anguish formed in my breast,
I prayed to God:
May I find support at the appointed place;
May I find a hero among the Muslims.
Against Kongurbay, son of Alooke,
I will unleash a great tumult;
I will turn and attack the swine
And take my ancient revenge.
So I have long prayed.
If I meet him in a lonely place,
I will offer the mother-forsaken Manchu
As a sacrifice,"
Kongurbay, who has long borne a grudge,
Has come here himself;
The time has come for me
To contend with that dog.
Raise your palms and give your blessing;
At the swaggering Kalmyk
I shall charge and thrust my spear,
With that grim-faced Kalmyk
I shall fight to the finish.
Before all the people we shall clash,
And I shall settle the quarrel once for all;
Before the nation we shall grapple,
And I shall ease my pent-up grief.
At that Kalmyk huge as Opol-Too
I shall level and stretch out my spear;
For this wretched life, so dearly troubled,
I shall find some course at last.
Against the blustering Kalmyk
Let me meet him face to face.
If my death has come, here is my life;
If fate has arrived, let me die.
The decree that God has written—
With this man, this mortal soul of mine
Will close in combat and see.
Before the people we shall joust,
And I shall firmly prove my valor;
From the infidel, for our ancient feud,
I shall take revenge this very moment.
You handful of Muslims,
Raise your palms and give your blessing;
I shall grip the yellow spear and spur myself on.
You handful of Muslims,
Thus I ask you to guard my honor;
If fortune favors me, the infidel
I shall drive all the way to Kakan.
I speak my farewell while I am safe;
With this dog standing here
I shall return after trading battle cries.
There will be spear-play, a true fight—
Thus I tell you my heart's longing.
At the pig who is the monks' khan
I shall stretch and thrust my spear.
Open your palms wide and bless me,
You handful of Muslims;
From the pig who is the monks' khan
I shall now take my revenge.
Spear in hand, breaking armor,
If my death has come, I shall fall to a bullet;
Against the grim black Chinese
I shall fight to the finish."
Ala-Mongku spoke these words,
Openly making his plea.
He readied himself to charge,
As wisdom came to him from the unseen.
His face looked like oiled wheat,
His eyes like the twilight mist.
The blood-drinker Manas, the panther,
The saint whom the patron spirit upheld,
Broad-chested, with a generous breast,
With great, imposing black eyes,
The brindled black panther,
Tensed along his flanks,
The stumpy-maned gray lion,
As though about to tear open a wound,
Gathered himself at the loins.
Your gray wolf of lofty spirit,
The panther blessed with matchless fortune—
When one looked upon his front,
He bore the majesty of six thousand men;
When he turned his back,
He had the aspect of a dragon.
No challenger had ever come against him,
No enemy he faced had gone unbeaten;
Hardened by a life of drinking blood,
He was famed as the black gray wolf.
Born in Altai, he grew mighty,
And his renown grew great.
Throughout all Kakan and Beijing
His heroism was known.
When he reached eight years of age,
"He will lay siege to Beijing," they said,
And in the records of Beijing's old khan
It was written down.
When he reached nine years of age,
He rode out to wage war on the foe.
"He will bring calamity," they said,
And one account of Manas
In the records of Beijing's old khan
Was entered and preserved.
When he came to the age of ten,
He boldly went out and fired his bow,
Destroying whoever faced him.
When he reached eleven,
He began the tumultuous battle;
Unable to withstand his wrath,
The black Chinese and the many Manchus
Broke ranks and fled away.
When he reached twelve,
He stormed a palace and took booty.
When he reached thirteen,
He shot the white maral and made it tame;
The black Kalmyks and Manchus
He drove about and made obedient.
He shot the blue maral and made it tame,
And subjected every land he sought.
When he reached fourteen,
They barely escaped with their lives.
If there was a giant on the earth,
He traveled in search of him to fight.
Whenever a fierce quarrel arose,
Among the black Kalmyks and Manchus
He laid their champions low.
When they provoked his stubborn wrath,
The insolent monks came of age;
When he unleashed his fury,
He made them call him "blood-drinking Burut,"
And began the tumultuous battle.
Bakburchu of Chinmachin,
When he learned the truth of Manas,
Was utterly shattered.
The mighty men of the coat-clad Chinese
Roared aloud,
Yet none dared advance and face him;
Against the hero Manas
Across the whole face of the earth
No one remained to twirl a lasso.
His fortune was perfectly balanced;
If you looked within him,
He was broader than the whole earth.
When he reached fifteen,
He found a land like Talas,
And found the Argyn and Kyrgyz people.
He devastated the Kyzylbash realm
And made its girls and women weep.
No land remained anywhere
That the racehorse Akkula had not trodden;
No people remained whole
Who had not heard his battle cry.
He broke through Ombu and opened a road,
And took booty from many lands.
He entered the Caliph's court and received a writ,
And received a blessing from the prince.
He raised strife in many lands,
And throughout Kakan and Beijing
He came to be called blood-drinking Manas.
Kongurbay, son of Alooke,
Without even racing Algara,
Had taken the prize away;
The merciless turmoil
Had then been set in motion.
When Akkula was entered in the race,
Your gray-wolf lion Manas
Was left with nothing.
The hero Manas lamented:
"Accursed, faithless world—
Why did I have to find you,
Foal of the bay mare,
Fleetest of the black herd,
Akkula, whom I ride into battle—
Why did I insist on racing him?
The black Chinese and the Manchus—
Their prowess, before my own eyes,
I had held for nothing;
That blood-drinker, the infidel Kongurbay,
That hero whose wrath is full,
Would enter this joust—
I had failed to understand it."
While Manas stood speaking thus,
His thoughts, it seemed, were divided.
Kanykei, the gray wolf's wife,
Appeared like the whole world,
Kanykei, mistress of every craft,
Showing the whiteness beneath her chin,
Her white breast gleaming,
Spoke softly and said this.
Having caused much bustle,
She finished it that very day.
The blood-drinker's Akolpok armor
She lifted up then
And had it brought to Akayar.
Beauty of the dark-bay folk,
Radiance of the Muslims,
